At the conclusion ofthe 139th Conven
tion, each delegate was asked to complete
a questionnaire evaluating the proceed
ings. One question asked, "What wfll you
remember as the high point of the 139th
Convention?" Some ofthe responses elic
ited were;
Getting to know brothers and sharing
common bonds.
Fellowship and cooperation.
The warmth and brotherly feeling .
These same thoughts were expressed in
various ways by many brothers. But one
undergraduate answered it best when he
succinctly said:
The whole thing!
By all standards, the 139th Conven
tion, hosted by the Lambda Chapter at
Columbia University in New York City
from August 18 through 21, was a huge
success! It provided a perfect blend of
hard work and good times, a balanced
combination not always easily attained.
Lambda undergraduates, ably led by
Peter Marullo '83, Undergraduate Con
vention Chairman, and Mike Fortine '83,
House Manager, had been busy all sum
mer
painting their house both inside and
out, refinishing floors, replacing doors,
paneling walls, and cleaning (even the
oven was immaculate), in preparation for
I their guests. The results of their efibrts
were best described by Henry B. Poor,
Gamma '39, Executive Vice President,
'
who dubbed it "The Miracle of 114th
I
Street ." Even those who had not seen the
I "before" were impressed with the "af^
ter.
"
Delegates began arriving on Wednes
day afternoon to register and check into
their rooms at Hartley Hall, a recently
remodeled dormitory donated by Marcellus Hartley Dodge, Lambda '03. The
tone of the next three days was set that
evening at the orientation meeting,
where Henry Poor expertly informed
"first-timers," as wefl as "old-hands," on
what they could expect from the Conven
tion and what, in turn, was expected of
them. His enthusiasm was contagious!
Following the orientation meeting,
undergraduates were
grouped by com
mon Chapter characteristics to facilitate
discussion of mutual concerns, while the
Executive Committee held its brain
storming session in anticipation of the
next day's Executive Council meeting.
That evening's open house at the Chapter
House provided the perfect informal
atmosphere for reminiscing about the
past with old friends and looking toward
the future with newly-made ones.
Despite the early hour (7:30 a.m. was
thought by many to be an inhuman time),
delegates gathered at the House on
Thursday morning, as on each succeeding
morning, for a Continental breakfast re
plete with all manner of delectable
viands, before commencing the full day of
meetings. It was especially appropriate
that all business sessions were conducted
in Ferris Booth Hall, a building named in
honor of a prominent member of the
Lambda Chapter, Class of '24. Under
graduates proceeded to educational
workshops on such topics as Chapter fi
nances, membership recruitment, alum
ni relations, and leadership skills de
velopment and then to divisional confer
ences. These sessions were superbly
moderated by six recent alumni: Lou
Brusco, Lambda'81; Mike Crane, Omega
'79 (former Field Director); Dick Dadey,
Pi '80 (present Field Director); Scott
Downs, Omega '79; Andy Kerstein, Del
ta '76; and Bill King, Omicron '73.
At the Executive Council's summer
meeting, reports were given by ofiicers,
committee chairmen, and staff members
on Annual Giving results and projections,
recent staff appointments, status of in
vestments, office operations, etc. Discus
sions ensued on the 1982-83 operating
budget, the realignment of the Executive
Council, an appropriate celebration of
the Fraternity's 150th anniversary, and
the status of the Chi Chapter at Comefl
University. Concrete decisions were
reached and passed on to standing com
mittees for Convention action.
Dr. Fritz R. Stern, Provost of Co
lumbia University, officially welcomed
Psi Upsflon Fraternity to the Columbia
campus at the opening luncheon that
noontime. He spoke of the tremendous
respect in which the Lambda Chapter is
held at his institution and the numerous
contributions its members have made
over the years to Columbia.
The 139th Convention of Psi Upsilon
Fraternity officially convened at 2:00
p.m. when Murray Eskenazi, Lambda
'56, President of the Lambda Alumni
Association and General Convention
Chairman, opened the first general meet
ing with words of greeting on behalf ofhis
Chapter and the Convention Committee.

Executive Council (a State of the Union
address, if you will) read by its President,

We come to college for an educa

ing the "truth."
I have found that there are few
absolute truths. Some truths are rel
atively stronger than others depend
ing upon the time, the place, the cir
cumstances, and the vision ofthe per
son seeking the truth.
Hitler saw truth one way. Churchill
saw the truth another way. Einstein
saw a relative truth. Nixon knew a
flexible truth (now you see it, now you
don't).
Karl Marx saw the truth, Cornelius
Vanderbilt saw the truth, St. Augus
tine saw the truth, and so did Thomas
Jefferson.
Confucius, Buddha, Moses, Jesus,
the Dalai Lama, St. Peter, Muham
mad, Billy Graham, and Reverend
Moon all saw the truth. I wonder,
were they all looking at the same
world?
Some truths endure longer than
others. They give continuity and
meaning to our lives. They provide us
with a formula or framework for living.
These truths may vary slightly from
person to person but it doesn't matter
�
as long as we can structure our lives
by them.
So tonight I offer you truth-seekers
a special treat. For one performance
only: The Four Gospels of Saint Mur
ray the Lambda.
TRUTH #1: You must aim for
perfection in order to achieve excel
lence. Our society has stopped aiming
high. We instead seek to meet mini
mum standards of acceptance �
to get
by is acceptable. A product like Rolls
Royce is no accident. Rolls Royce got
to where it is and built its reputation
by being demanding. By seeking
perfection, one often attains excel
lence.
TRUTH #2: In voluntary groups,
20% ofthe people do 90% ofthe work.
Fratemities are a prime example of
You can afl think of more instances
than I can. Sometimes, just recogniz
ing that a job should be done which is
going undone is what separates the
20% of workers fi-om the 80% of shirk
ers.
TRUTH #3: Over 300 years ago, an
Enghshman named John Locke wrote:
All that is necessaryfor the triumph of
evil isfor enough good men to do noth
ing . This says so much in so few words.
In fraternity life, in business, in
public life, when the good men sit
idle, then the base and venal men mn
things. Whole societies have deterio
rated and empires have faflen because
the good men did nothing.
TRUTH #4 (and this one is most
obvious): Murray ain't a Saint.
I ask you, in your personal lives and
in your fraternity lives, to aim high, to
seek perfection in order to achieve the
excellence that being a Psi U de
mands.
By your presence here at this Con
vention you have indicated that you
are part of the 20% that does 90% of
the work. Don't shirk the work. Or
you'll regret not doing what your in
stincts and nature told you should
have been done.
I hope you will be one of those good
guys who cannot sit idle while the bad
guys do their job. Speak out strongly!
You will be amazed at the number of
times you will triumph for the good
guys. The Force of Goodness is much
stronger than the Force of Evil �
all
you have to do is USE it.
And that's the Gospel according to
Saint Murray the Lambda. I am look
ing forward to meeting all of you next
year at the Sesquicentennial celebra
tion of the finest Fraternity on God's
green earth.

New High Reached in 1981-82 Annual
Giving Program
Once again the alumni of Psi Upsilon, some of the
most loyal and supportive in the fraternity world, have set
a new record in gift giving. The 1981-82 Annual Giving
results show $83,016 donated by 1,937 contributors,
for an average gift of $42.86. This represents an in
crease over last year's figures of almost $7,000, with the
average size of each gift rising by over $3. During this
time of recession, this is truly a remarkable accomplish
ment.
The following statistics and lists serve to honor the
faithful alumni who, by their generosity, have enabled
Psi Upsilon to expand the scope of its services and activi
ties in behalf of our undergraduate chapters. The Execu
tive Council extends heartiest thanks for each measure of
assistance, large and small.
In this, Psi Upsilon's 150th year, we must ask our
alumni to raise their sights still further so that we can
continue to perpetuate what is recognized as one of the
finest fraternities. The 1982-83 operating budget calls
for $93,500 in Annual Giving contributions. Of great
encouragement is the fact that this year's program is off
to a resounding start. We think that the alumni of Psi
Upsilon once again will rise to the challenge of meeting,
perhaps even exceeding, this goal!

Pi's Reunite in Boston
On May 8 the brotherhood of the Pi
Chapter held a reunion "of sorts" at the
Boston apartment of Brother Kent
Damon, Pi '65. The get-together was
planned to celebrate what was once
Clambake Weekend at the Pi and to re
new old acquaintances.
The gala was organized by a
steering
(no bull!) committee of Pi brothers, in
cluding Kent Damon '65, Frank DiMella
'65, Tuck Nichols '65, Phil Quartier '65,
and George Whitehead '65. Lest one
think this was only a Class of '65 affair, it
should be reported that the idea for the
reunion was that of Bob Bender '64, who
quickly delegated the organization to the
"underclassmen." Jeff Low '63 did the
artwork for the invitations, and George
Whitehead '65 did most ofthe grunt work
of tracking down wayward brothers.
Twenty-five members ofthe Classes of
'62 through '66 could be found playing
Wales-tales and partaking in a
group sere
nade. Psi U Days and Bold and Ready
were
sung with gusto, while Brothers All
evoked tears in many an eye.
All in all it was a memorable evening,
bringing many laughs, a few tears, and
even an occasional confession. It is hoped
that this spirit can be rekindled at future
